messages.content: I'm setting up books for my new design studio. I put $5,000 of my own money into the business bank account. Everyone says a journal entry needs two sides - can you show me what this one actually looks like in tables, and prove it's balanced?
I'll build the smallest honest ledger - an accounts table, a journals table, and a lines table where every amount is integer cents - and record your contribution as journal 1:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE accounts (account_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, type TEXT NOT NULL)

messages.name: database_query
messages.content: {"status": "ok"}

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE journals (journal_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, journal_date TEXT NOT NULL, memo TEXT NOT NULL)

messages.name: database_query
messages.content: {"status": "ok"}

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE journal_lines (journal_id INTEGER NOT NULL, line_no INTEGER NOT NULL, account_id INTEGER NOT NULL, debit_cents INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0, credit_cents INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0)

messages.name: database_query
messages.content: {"status": "ok"}

messages.name: database_query

messages.name: database_query

messages.name: database_query
messages.content: 2 row(s) affected
The entry is in. Here are its lines with account names, and then the balance proof - total debits against total credits across the whole ledger:

arguments.sql: SELECT a.name AS account, l.debit_cents, l.credit_cents FROM journal_lines l JOIN accounts a ON a.account_id = l.account_id WHERE l.journal_id = 1 ORDER BY l.line_no

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
account | debit_cents | credit_cents
Cash | 500000 | 0
Owner Capital | 0 | 500000

arguments.sql: SELECT SUM(debit_cents) AS total_debits, SUM(credit_cents) AS total_credits FROM journal_lines

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
total_debits | total_credits
500000 | 500000

Read the entry as a sentence: debit Cash 500000, credit Owner Capital 500000 - in dollars, the business received $5,000.00 of cash, and the source of that cash is your ownership stake. Debit and credit are not 'good' and 'bad', or even 'in' and 'out' - they are the left and right side of an entry, and the rule that makes the whole system work is the one the second query just proved: total debits (500000) equal total credits (500000). Cash is an asset, and assets are debit-normal, meaning a debit increases them. Owner Capital is equity, which is credit-normal, so the credit side is what increases it. Every entry you ever record will have this shape: at least one debit line and one credit line, and the two sides equal to the cent. Get that invariant right and the reports built on top of these tables can be trusted; break it once and every total downstream is quietly wrong.
First sale today - a client paid $1,200 cash for a logo package. If cash goes up with a debit, what happens on the other side? The money came from a sale, not from me.
Exactly right - the other side names where the value came from. A sale earns revenue, and revenue is credit-normal, so the credit goes to Sales Revenue:

Now the balances, computed the same way for both accounts - each account's balance is the sum over its lines, taken on its normal side (debits minus credits for an asset, credits minus debits for revenue):

arguments.sql: SELECT a.name AS account, SUM(CASE WHEN a.type IN ('asset', 'expense') THEN l.debit_cents - l.credit_cents ELSE l.credit_cents - l.debit_cents END) AS balance_cents FROM accounts a JOIN journal_lines l ON l.account_id = a.account_id GROUP BY a.name ORDER BY a.account_id

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
account | balance_cents
Cash | 120000
Sales Revenue | 120000

Both accounts read 120000 - $1,200.00 of cash on hand, and $1,200.00 of revenue earned. Notice the two balances being equal is a coincidence of this being the only entry; what is not a coincidence is the pattern. There are five account types and each has a normal side: assets and expenses are debit-normal (debits increase them), while liabilities, equity, and revenue are credit-normal (credits increase them). Revenue being credit-normal feels backwards to most people at first - you 'earn' money, so why credit? Because the credit side of an entry answers 'where did the value come from', and revenue is a source of value to the business, just like your capital contribution was. The debit side answers 'where did the value go'. Keep those two questions straight and you can construct almost any entry yourself.
I paid this month's studio rent, $950, out of the business account. I already have my $5,000 contribution in the books. Record the rent and show me the whole picture still balances.

The picture: Cash is 405000 cents - $5,000.00 in, $950.00 out, $4,050.00 left. Rent Expense stands at 95000 ($950.00), Owner Capital at 500000 ($5,000.00). And the trial balance ties: total debits 595000 equal total credits 595000. That check has a name because it is the oldest error-detector in bookkeeping - if anyone ever keys one side of an entry wrong, or drops a line, the two totals disagree and you know it before any report goes out. Notice what the rent entry did to the shape of the business: an asset (cash) shrank and an expense grew. Expenses growing is not the ledger 'losing' money in a mysterious place - the expense account is precisely where the cost of running the studio accumulates, so that at month end you can subtract total expenses from total revenue and get an honest profit figure.
I keep reading that 'debit means increase and credit means decrease'. Then my bookkeeper says a credit increased our revenue. One of them has to be wrong - which is it?

Your bookkeeper is right, and the slogan is the thing that's wrong. Debit and credit, at bottom, mean only left and right - the two columns of an entry. Whether a debit increases or decreases an account depends entirely on the account's type, because each type has a 'normal side' where its balance grows:

- Assets (cash, equipment, money owed to you): debit-normal. A debit increases them.
- Expenses (rent, wages, supplies used): debit-normal. A debit increases them.
- Liabilities (loans, bills you owe): credit-normal. A credit increases them.
- Equity (owner's stake): credit-normal. A credit increases it.
- Revenue (sales): credit-normal. A credit increases it.

So a debit increases cash but decreases a loan balance - when you pay $200 toward a loan, you credit Cash (asset down) and debit the loan (liability down). Same word, opposite effect, because the accounts face opposite directions. There's a logic to the split: assets and expenses are things the business has or consumes - they live on the left of the accounting equation. Liabilities, equity, and revenue are claims on and sources of those assets - they live on the right. If the slogan helps you, replace it with this one: a debit increases anything on the asset/expense side and decreases anything on the liability/equity/revenue side; a credit does the reverse. It is less catchy, but unlike the short version, it is never wrong.
Our spreadsheet import drops journal lines into a staging table before they post to the ledger. Something looks off this month - can you check the staged journals for balance before anything posts?

Good instinct - staging is exactly where you want to catch this, because staged lines are still drafts. The check is per journal: sum the debits, sum the credits, and flag any journal where they differ:

journal_id | debits | credits | diff

messages.name: database_query

messages.name: database_query

messages.name: database_query

total_debits | total_credits
397500 | 397500

The flag query now returns no rows at all - just its header - and the totals tie at 397500 on both sides. Three lessons in this small hunt. First, check balance per journal, not just in total: a +45000 error in one journal and a -45000 error in another would cancel in the grand total and sail through. Second, the size of the difference is diagnostic - here it was exactly the missing line's amount, which told us a whole line was absent rather than mistyped. Third, notice where the fix was allowed to happen: in staging, before posting. Once lines post to the real ledger they are history, and corrections there take a different form - a new, balanced correcting entry - never an edit. Staging is the one place in the pipeline where 'just fix the row' is the right answer.

Final state: Accounts Payable reads 0 - the debt existed, and then it was settled, and the ledger shows both facts instead of pretending the supplies were free. Cash is 66000 ($1,000.00 in, $340.00 out), Supplies stand at 34000, and your capital is untouched at 100000. This two-step pattern is the whole point of accounts payable as an account: between the two entries, anyone reading the books could see exactly what the business owed and to the cent. If you'd recorded only the payment, the books would show cash leaving for no stated reason; if you'd recorded the purchase as a cash buy, cash would have looked $340 lighter during two weeks when it wasn't. The liability account is what makes the timing honest.
A customer paid me $200 cash for a repair. Why can't I just add $200 to the Cash account and be done? The two-line thing feels like ceremony.

It feels like ceremony until you watch what the one-line version does to the accounting equation. Your books, before the payment, are in balance: say assets of $5,000 (the cash in the account) against equity of $5,000 - Assets = Liabilities + Equity, 5,000 = 0 + 5,000. Now do it your way and just add $200 to Cash. Assets become $5,200, equity is still $5,000, and the equation reads 5,200 = 5,000 - broken, by exactly the $200 you added. That gap isn't pedantry; it's the books claiming $200 exists that came from nowhere. Every report built on those numbers now quietly overstates what you own relative to what you earned and owe.

The two-line entry is what keeps the story complete: debit Cash $200 (the value arrived, as cash), credit Repair Revenue $200 (the value came from work you sold). Assets rise to $5,200 and equity rises to $5,200 too - revenue flows into equity at the end of the period - and the equation holds. The second line is not a copy of the first; it answers a different question. Line one says where the value is now. Line two says where it came from. Drop either answer and some future question - 'how much did we actually earn this month?' or 'why does the bank balance not match our sales?' - becomes unanswerable from the books. The ceremony is two lines long because the truth has two halves.
I took $600 out of the business account for personal use. My instinct is to book it as an expense - money went out, right? My bookkeeper says no. Why not?

Your bookkeeper is right, and the distinction matters every time you look at your profit. The entry is: debit Drawings 60000, credit Cash 60000 - in dollars, $600.00 out of cash, recorded against an account called Drawings. Drawings is a contra-equity account: it sits inside equity, facing the other way, accumulating what you've pulled out of the business for yourself.

Here's why it must not be an expense. Expenses are the costs of earning revenue - rent, wages, materials. Profit is revenue minus those costs, and it's the number you use to judge whether the business works. Suppose the month shows revenue of $3,000.00 and true expenses of $1,800.00: profit is $1,200.00. That figure is identical whether you drew $600, drew nothing, or drew $2,000 - because your personal withdrawals are not a cost of earning anything; they're you, the owner, taking your share of the results after the fact. Book the $600 as an expense and profit drops to a fake $600.00, and now the books say the business is half as healthy as it really is - which can scare a lender, mislead a partner, or talk you out of a good decision. What the draw does reduce is your equity: capital contributed minus drawings (plus accumulated profit) is your actual stake. The draw is real, it's recorded, it just lives in the equity story rather than the profit story.

The bank lent my business $10,000. Then the first monthly payment of $350 came out - the statement says $290 of it was principal and $60 was interest. I don't see how one payment becomes an entry when it splits two ways.

The loan arriving is the easy half: cash up, debt up. The payment is a three-line entry, and three lines are fine - the rule is only that debits equal credits, not that there are exactly two lines. First the loan:

That separation is the entire reason for the split: if you'd debited the whole $350 to the loan, the books would claim you owe $9,650.00 - $60 less than the bank says - and the cost of borrowing would vanish from your expenses, flattering your profit. Principal is a balance-sheet movement (debt becoming smaller); interest is a profit-and-loss cost (the price of having the money). One payment, two different stories, and the three-line entry tells both.

I'm trying to get fluent at reading journal entries. Here are three from our books - can you translate each into a plain sentence about what actually happened? (1) Debit Cash 25000, Credit Sales Revenue 25000. (2) Debit Equipment 180000, Credit Cash 60000, Credit Notes Payable 120000. (3) Debit Wages Expense 43000, Credit Cash 43000. All amounts are cents.

Gladly - and the method is always the same: the debit side says what the business got or consumed, the credit side says what it gave up or where the value came from.

(1) 'We sold something for $250.00 and the customer paid cash.' Cash went up $250.00 (debit, asset increasing), and the source was a sale - revenue credited $250.00. One event, two halves: money in the drawer, earnings on the books.

(2) 'We bought equipment priced at $1,800.00, paid $600.00 of it in cash on the spot, and financed the remaining $1,200.00.' Equipment - an asset - increases by the full $1,800.00, because the business owns the whole machine today, not just the paid-for slice. The credits split because the value came from two sources: $600.00 of cash left the account, and a $1,200.00 debt was created. Debits 180000, credits 60000 + 120000 = 180000 - balanced, as always.

(3) 'We paid $430.00 of wages in cash.' The debit lands on Wages Expense - labor was consumed earning revenue - and cash falls by the same $430.00.

Notice entry (2) is the one that trips people: an entry may have one debit and several credits, or the reverse, whenever value genuinely arrives from or goes to more than one place. The invariant never changes - the two sides sum to the same total - only the number of lines telling the story does.

The fix is not to hand-edit 359000 into 386500 - it's to recompute the cache from the entries, and then fix the import path so the next settlement updates it too. A stored balance that disagrees with its own ledger isn't a balance at all; it's a rumor with a number attached.

Be honest - isn't deriving the balance from entries every time just slow purism? Every banking app I've used shows a balance instantly. Stored must be fine.

Stored is fine - as long as you're honest about what it is: a cache. The entries are the balance; a stored figure is a precomputed answer to 'what do the entries sum to?' kept around because asking is expensive. Caches are respectable engineering. What gets people hurt is treating the cache as the truth and the entries as decoration.

Three conditions make a stored balance safe. First, a rebuild path: a job that can throw the stored figure away and recompute it from entries, run on a schedule and after any incident - if you can't rebuild it, you don't have a cache, you have a second ledger that will eventually disagree with the first. Second, drift monitoring: a periodic check that stored equals derived, with a difference treated as a bug to find, not a number to patch - the difference is always information, usually a code path that posted an entry without updating the cache. Third, one writer discipline: the stored figure is updated in the same transaction as the entry insert, or not trusted at all. Where people get into real trouble is the pattern 'the app usually updates it' - usually is where the missing $275 lives. So no, it isn't purism. Derive when the volume allows it, because then the question never arises. Cache when you must, with rebuilds and drift checks, and let the entries win every argument.
Two weird balances on our report. Cash shows negative $120, and our Repairs Expense account shows a negative balance too - I thought expenses only go up. Are both of these bugs?

Different animals - one is a fire alarm, the other is just the ledger reporting honestly. Cash at negative $120 means the entries claim you paid out $120 more than ever came in. For a real bank account that's impossible unless the account is genuinely overdrawn, so treat it as an investigation, not a display quirk: either a payment was recorded twice, a receipt was never recorded, or a payment was recorded against the wrong account. The derived balance can't 'go wrong' - it can only faithfully total entries that are themselves wrong, and a negative cash balance is often the first visible symptom.

The expense account is different. Suppose Repairs Expense holds $250.00 of repair bills, and then a $300.00 refund lands from a supplier for a part that was returned - recorded, correctly, as a credit against the same expense account. The derived balance is now negative $50.00: 25000 - 30000 = -5000 cents. Nothing is broken. The account is telling you that this period, refunds exceeded repair spending by fifty dollars - a true fact, and arguably useful. The general rule: a balance on the 'wrong' side of an account's normal side is the ledger raising its hand. For cash and receivables, it almost always means an entry error or a missing entry. For expense and revenue accounts, it usually means a reversal, refund, or correction exceeded the original activity - legitimate, but worth being able to explain line by line if anyone asks.

A supplier invoice from last month was recorded as $540 but it was really $450. Why is everyone so dramatic about not just editing the entry? It's one digit.

Because that one digit is load-bearing in more places than the entry itself. The $540 figure has already flowed into last month's expense total, the cash balance as of last month's end, the reconciliation against last month's bank statement, and possibly a report someone already sent. Edit the entry in place and all of those become silently different from what anyone saw at the time - the bank reconciliation that balanced last month no longer balances, and nobody can tell whether the books changed or their memory is wrong. An edited ledger can't prove its own past.

The append-only rule is the alternative: history is never rewritten, only answered. You post a new entry, dated today, that reverses the wrong one in full, and a second new entry that records the correct $450. The journal now shows all three events - the mistake, its reversal, the correction - and anyone auditing can follow the whole story. Reports for last month still reproduce exactly as they were, because 'as of' a posting date the wrong entry was the latest word; reports as of today show the corrected picture. It costs you two extra entries and a sentence of memo. What it buys is the property everything else in bookkeeping leans on: any number anyone ever quoted can be re-derived and explained. The moment edits are allowed, every number needs the follow-up question '...as of when you last looked?' - and nobody can answer it.

I deposited $4,150 at the branch on October 31 and logged it in our books that day. The October statement doesn't show it - it appears November 2. My reconciliation is off by exactly $4,150 and my software keeps flagging it as an error. Is it one?

No - it's the most ordinary reconciling item there is, and your software is flagging a difference it doesn't understand the species of. Walk the timeline. On October 31, two records are created: the bank has your money (you handed it over; their internal ledger knows), and your books record the deposit. But the statement is a snapshot of what the bank had processed by its cutoff, and your deposit landed after it - so the October statement closes at, say, $12,083.00 without it, while your books close at $16,233.00, with it. The difference is exactly the deposit, $4,150.00, and the reconciliation handles it by adjusting the bank side: statement $12,083.00 + deposit in transit $4,150.00 = $16,233.00, which ties to the books. Nothing gets edited on either side.

The defining trait of a deposit in transit is that it heals itself: on the November statement it simply appears, dated November 2, and the item drops off the reconciliation list forever. That's also your verification - a genuine in-transit deposit always shows up within a few business days. If a 'deposit in transit' is still unaccounted for two statements later, it has stopped being a timing item and become a problem: the deposit was recorded in the books but never reached the bank (lost, misrouted, or - the case auditors look for - recorded to cover a shortage elsewhere). Rule of thumb: timing items are young or they're suspects. Reconcile them by listing and adjusting, never by deleting the book entry to match the statement - the books are right about what you did; the statement just hasn't caught up.
When the books and the bank disagree, how do I decide whether to change our books, or just note it and move on? I never know which side is 'wrong'.

Sort the difference into one of three species first - the species decides who adjusts.

Species one: timing. Checks you've written that haven't cleared; deposits you've made that haven't posted. Neither side is wrong - the bank statement is a photograph taken mid-motion. These never change the books. They adjust the bank side of the reconciliation (statement balance minus outstanding checks plus deposits in transit) and they should clear themselves on the next statement. An old timing item that never clears graduates to an investigation.

Species two: bank-only items. Service fees, interest earned, an automatic payment the bank ran that nobody booked. The bank is right - the money really moved - and the books are incomplete. These always adjust the books: you record the fee as an expense or the interest as revenue, and then the difference is gone because the books now contain the event.

Species three: errors - and here you ask whose. A check you keyed as $540 that cleared at $450 is your error: fix the books (with a correcting entry, not an edit). A check that cleared at an amount different from what you actually wrote is the bank's error: you change nothing, you notify the bank, and the item rides the reconciliation until they fix it. The master principle underneath all three: the bank is the authority on what has cleared your account; the books are the authority on what you intended to do. Most reconciliation confusion comes from asking one of them to be the authority on the other's subject.

How often are we actually supposed to reconcile? Our bookkeeper does it at tax time and it takes her a week of archaeology. There's got to be a better rhythm.

There is, and the archaeology is the symptom of skipping it. The standard rhythm is monthly, tied to the bank statement: the statement arrives, you reconcile to it, and the close isn't done until the two agree with every difference named. Monthly works because the evidence is still warm - a three-week-old deposit in transit can be traced; a fourteen-month-old one is a research project, and the people who might remember it have forgotten or left. For an account with heavy daily volume, weekly is worth it: the item list stays short, a duplicate or a missing settlement surfaces within days while the source documents are still on someone's desk, and the month-end close becomes a formality instead of an excavation.

Two habits matter as much as the frequency. Reconcile to the statement, not to zero: the target is the bank's adjusted balance, computed from the statement plus your known timing items - 'the difference is zero' means nothing if both sides are being bent toward it. And keep the reconciliations: each one is a dated proof that on that day, these books matched that statement with these named items outstanding. A year of those is a control an auditor can lean on; a single heroic tax-time reconciliation is a story. The week your bookkeeper spends is the interest on a year of skipped months - the principal was always about twenty minutes a month.

Last month we dunned a client for an invoice our system said was unpaid. They'd paid three weeks earlier - a staffer had recorded the payment but the invoice still said 'unpaid'. My co-owner says the fix is a checklist so nobody forgets to flip the status. I suspect you'd say something else.

Your suspicion is correct: the checklist treats the symptom, and it will fail again the first week someone is busy, sick, or new. The root defect is architectural - your system stores a claim ('status: unpaid') in one place and the evidence (payments) in another, and relies on human memory to keep them synchronized. Every synchronization that depends on memory eventually desynchronizes; the only question is whether it desynchronizes toward dunning a client who paid, or toward writing off a client who never did.

The fix is to delete the claim and derive the fact. An invoice's status is fully determined by two numbers that already exist: the invoice total and the sum of its payments. Zero paid: unpaid. Some paid: partial, with the balance right there. All paid: paid. Computed on read, it cannot disagree with the payments because it IS the payments, summarized. The same disease - a stored summary drifting from the events it summarizes - is behind most 'the system says X but reality says Y' bugs in business software: inventory counts nobody can reproduce, balances nobody can re-derive, 'customer since' dates that were typed once. The pattern to learn is: when a human complains that a field is 'wrong half the time', don't add process around the field. Ask whether the field should exist at all, or whether it's a view waiting to be written.

Don't edit the invoice - answer it with a second document: a credit note for 8600 cents, referencing invoice, client, and reason ('rush fee charged in error'). The invoice stays exactly as issued at 48600; the credit note stands beside it at -8600; and the balance due is the sum of the two documents: 48600 - 8600 = 40000 - $400.00, which is what the client should pay. Two documents, one truth, and the arithmetic is checkable by anyone holding both pages.

Why not just fix the invoice? Because the invoice has already left the building - the client has a copy that says $486.00. If your copy quietly becomes $400.00, the two of you now hold different versions of the same numbered document, and any later disagreement starts from 'your records don't match mine'. With a credit note, both parties' paper agrees: the original invoice at $486.00, the credit note at -$86.00, the balance at $400.00. The error is visible rather than airbrushed, which paradoxically makes you look better - a business that documents its corrections is more trustworthy than one whose documents are always suspiciously perfect. This is the same append-only instinct as the ledger itself, one level up: documents, like entries, are corrected by adding, never by rewriting. If the client had already paid the $486.00, the same credit note would instead create a $86.00 credit in their favor - applied to their next invoice or refunded - and the paper trail would tell that story too.

There is: stop storing fractions of an hour and bill in the unit that has no fractions - minutes. At $120.00 an hour, the per-minute rate is a whole number of cents: 12000 / 60 = 200 cents a minute. Now both calls price exactly. The 90-minute call: 90 x 200 = 18000 cents, $180.00. The 25-minute call: 25 x 200 = 5000 cents, $50.00. No decimals anywhere, nothing to round, nothing to drift.

Your app's problem is that 25 minutes is 0.41666... hours - an infinite decimal that gets truncated or stored as a float, and 0.4167 x $120 is $50.004, which rounds to $50.00 only sometimes and explains itself never. The general principle travels well beyond timesheets: store quantities in the smallest unit you'll ever bill, count, or measure - minutes not hours, cents not dollars, grams not kilos - and do the arithmetic on integers, where computers are exact. Convert to the friendly unit only at the moment of display, and round only there, once, where the reader can see it. If your rate ever stops dividing cleanly - say $100 an hour, which is 166.66... cents a minute - the same discipline still wins: price = round(minutes x rate_cents / 60) computed once per line, with the rounding visible on the invoice, instead of accumulated silently inside a stored decimal.

Real harm, and the tidiness is the trap. An invoice number is not a row label; it's the name of a document that existed in the world. Invoice 1043 was issued - the wrong client received it, possibly filed it, possibly has it in their accounts-payable system right now. If a second, different invoice also becomes 1043, then 'invoice 1043' names two different obligations, and every future reference - a payment stub, an email, a dispute - is ambiguous. Auditors read a reused number the way you'd read a reused check number: as a place where a document could be swapped.

The tidy sequence you're picturing is actually the suspicious one. A healthy sequence has gaps, and every gap has a one-word explanation: voided. Keep invoice 1043 in the system forever, marked void, with the reason ('issued to wrong client, reissued as 1044') recorded as an entry or a status derived from a void event - never deleted, never reassigned. Then the sequence tells a complete story: 1042 paid, 1043 voided and why, 1044 paid. Regulators in many places require exactly this - sequential numbering with voids retained - because the gap-free, gap-explained sequence is what makes it provable that no invoice was issued off the books. The number is cheap. The provability is the asset.

Explain the largest remainder method like I'm a smart person who has never split anything more complicated than a pizza. Why does it exist and how does it work?

It exists because of an awkward fact: money comes in whole cents, but fair shares usually don't. Split $10.01 three equal ways and fairness says 333.67 cents each - a share that cannot be paid. Every real-world split is a negotiation between the exact shares arithmetic wants and the whole cents reality allows, and largest remainder is the fairest known way to run that negotiation.

The method has four steps. One: compute everyone's exact share, fractions and all. Two: give everyone the floor of their share - the whole cents just under it (333 each, in our example). You've now distributed 999 of the 1001 cents and nobody has more than they should. Three: count the leftover cents - here, 2. Four: hand the leftovers out one each to the shares with the largest fractional remainders - the people who lost the most to flooring. Our three shares all have the same fraction (.67), so the tie breaks by any stated order - first two listed, say - giving 334, 334, 333. Sum: exactly 1001.

Why this method and not just 'round each share normally'? Because independent rounding can create or destroy money: three shares of 333.67 round to 334 each, totaling 1002 - a cent conjured from nothing, which a payout system then has to take from somewhere. Largest remainder can never do that: floors start at or below the total, and you distribute at most the exact leftover. It's used anywhere shares must be both proportional and exact - tip pools, revenue splits, syndicate winnings, even seats in some parliaments. The pizza version: when the last slice can't be divided equally, it goes to whoever got the smallest piece so far. That's the whole idea.

Second, reconciliation: last month's reconciliation balanced against a set of lines that included that row; delete it and last month no longer reconciles, retroactively, with no way to see why. Delete it and no past number can ever be re-derived; every figure you've ever stated becomes unverifiable, including the true ones.

The alternative costs almost nothing: leave the wrong row and post a reversing row that cancels it, with a memo saying what happened. The pair sums to zero in every total, and the story - mistake, discovery, correction - is fully visible. Rows in a ledger aren't like drafts in a document; they're more like entries in a ship's log. Our POS has both a VOID button and a REFUND button and the staff use them interchangeably. Settle it: what's the actual difference, in money terms?

The difference is whether the money ever settled. A void happens before settlement - typically the same day, often within hours. The card transaction was authorized but never captured into a completed batch, so voiding it releases the authorization and the charge simply never becomes real: no money moved, nothing to give back, and the books need at most a memo, because financially the sale evaporated before it existed. A refund happens after settlement - the batch closed, the money actually transferred from the customer's account to yours - so undoing it requires a second, real movement of money back, with its own fees, its own timeline (days, usually), and its own ledger entries: revenue reversed, cash or clearing credited.

The practical consequences of confusing them: voiding what should be a refund (or recording a refund for what was really a void) leaves the books claiming money moved when it didn't, or failing to claim money that did - and the drawer or the clearing account will be off by exactly that amount at reconciliation, with a very confusing paper trail. Timing is the test your staff can apply at the register: if the transaction is still in today's open batch, it's a void. If the customer has gone home, the batch has closed, or the charge appears on their statement - it's a refund, full stop. Same-day cash sales blur it slightly: cash 'settles' instantly, so a cash return is always effectively a refund with entries. The buttons aren't synonyms; they're two different points in the money's journey.

What you need is a small, new, balanced entry that moves exactly the misclassified amount between exactly the two accounts involved: debit Equipment 30000, credit Office Supplies 30000, with a memo that names the original journal and the reason ('reclass line 3 of journal 12 - equipment coded to supplies'). After it posts, Office Supplies is down the 30000 it never should have held, Equipment is up the 30000 it always should have, and every total that was right stays right - the entry is a pure reclassification: it changes no cash, no revenue, no expense total (supplies expense falls, but note equipment is an asset, so this one DOES change the expense total - correctly: the $300 was never an expense at all, it was a purchase of a durable asset, and that distinction is the whole point of the fix).

Why not reverse all four lines and re-enter? You could, and it would end in the same balances - but it would churn three correct lines through reversal and re-entry, tripling the surface for a new typo, and it would make the journal harder to read: the audit question 'what happened with the equipment purchase?' now has a nine-line answer instead of a five-line one. The discipline is proportional correction: reverse in full when the entry is wrong in its bones (wrong amount, wrong event), correct surgically when exactly one attribute is wrong and the correcting entry can name it. Either way, the original line is never edited - the correction is a new fact that references the old one.

Your partner is applying the rate like a taxi meter; your terms don't. 'Per month or part of a month' means any started month counts as a whole month - the fee is a step function, not a slope. The 45-day invoice has started two months of lateness (days 1-30 are month one; day 31 starts month two), so the fee is 84000 x 0.015 x 2 = 2520 cents - $25.20 - for a total due of $865.20. The 10-day invoice has started one month: 84000 x 0.015 = 1260 cents - $12.60 - total $852.60. The 2.25% figure would be right under different terms ('1.5% per month, prorated daily'), and under those terms the 10-day invoice would owe about a third of a month's fee instead of a full one. Neither is more correct in the abstract - but they are different contracts, and the invoice has to be computed by the one your terms actually state.

Compute the fee on the overdue balance, not the original invoice amount, if part has been paid - the terms say 'on overdue balances', and charging fees on money already received is how businesses end up refunding fees with apologies. And if the step function feels harsh at day 31, the remedy is to change the terms prospectively - many businesses soften it with a grace period ('no fee within 10 days of the due date') - not to prorate ad hoc for sympathetic clients. A fee rule that bends case by case isn't a rule; it's a negotiation, and clients compare notes.

Then the report says something true and useful: 'current' means nobody owes us anything they're late on, and anything beyond current is genuinely late by the agreement that client actually signed. One more refinement separates good aging reports from naive ones: a great payer on Net 60 who always pays on day 45 is paying 15 days EARLY by their terms - if your collections team is working from an invoice-date report, they're spending their worry on your best clients and ignoring the Net 10 client who is quietly 50 days past due. There's a second, sharper edge: allocation affects the client's legal position. In many places, a debtor who specifies an application gets it honored; a debtor who doesn't specify lets the creditor apply it - and the creditor's convention, once stated, binds. If your terms say payments apply oldest-first, applying one to the newest because of a passing mention isn't a bookkeeping preference, it's a deviation from your own stated policy that the client can later dispute ('I paid the January invoice - the March one is what I still owe, and it's not late'). So no, not a fuss over nothing. Pick the convention - oldest-first is the industry default for good reasons - publish it in your terms, and let the allocation table enforce it uniformly. Ad hoc allocation is how two honest people end up with two different ledgers for the same debt.

Be straight with me: besides making the accountant happy, what is an aging report actually FOR? We print it monthly and nobody does anything with it.

Then you're printing the menu and never ordering. An aging report has exactly one job: to produce this week's collection actions, in priority order, with the amounts attached. Read it as a queue, not a summary. The 90+ bucket is the decision list - every line there gets collected hard, settled for less, or written off this month, because a debt's collectibility decays with age and the 90+ column is where good money goes to become bad-debt expense. The 61-90 bucket is the conversation list: these clients get a call with a plan before they slide into the decision list. The 31-60 bucket is the nudge list - cheap, friendly, automated if you like. Current and 1-30 aren't collection items at all; they're the control group that tells you the system is working.

The second job is cash forecasting: the bucket totals, haircut by their historical collection rates, are a far better predictor of next month's receipts than the sales forecast is. If 90+ money historically pays at 30 cents on the dollar, then $18,000 in that bucket is $5,400 of expected cash, and planning as if it were $18,000 is how businesses miss payroll with a 'profitable' quarter on paper. So the monthly ritual should end with names and actions, not a printout: who calls whom, who gets a payment plan, who gets written off, and what the buckets say cash will actually look like. A report nobody acts on is worse than no report - it documents that you saw the problem coming and filed it.

The GROUP BY query is the whole fix, and it's a design principle, not a trick: a monetary amount is not a number, it's a number plus a currency, and arithmetic is only defined within one currency at a time. Every total in a multi-currency system is therefore either per-currency or explicitly converted with a stated rate - there is no third kind. The dashboard bug is the dangerous kind: it didn't crash, it produced a plausible-looking figure. If your system lets a query sum across currencies without complaint, the schema is missing its guardrail - many teams make the currency part of the account itself (Cash-USD, Cash-EUR) precisely so that a cross-currency sum becomes impossible to write by accident.

This matters because the alternative - storing only the dollar figure and 'remembering' the rate, or worse, re-converting historical euro amounts at whatever today's rate is - quietly rewrites history every time the market moves. A euro payment from March re-valued at December's rate would show a different dollar amount than the one that actually hit the bank, and the reconciliation with the March bank statement would break for no visible reason. Historical rates are unrecoverable later: nobody can tell you what rate your bank applied on a Tuesday in March unless the entry says so. So the entry says so - amount in, rate applied, amount out, all three, always. The rate's source (bank's actual rate, central bank reference, card network rate) belongs in the row too when there are several candidates; the one thing the future cannot do is guess which one you used.

Each EUR 33.33 x 1.08 = 3599.64, which rounds to 3600 - three roundings, each upward, total 10800. The bulk conversion rounds once:

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
bulk_total_usd
10799

Bulk: 9999 x 1.08 = 10798.92, rounding to 10799. One cent apart, and the mechanism is fully understood: per-receipt rounding threw away -0.36 of a cent three times in your favor... more precisely, it rounded 3599.64 up to 3600 three times, gaining 0.36 x 3 = 1.08 cents of rounding, while bulk rounded 10798.92 up once, gaining 0.08. The difference between the policies is accumulated rounding, and it grows with transaction count - at thousands of receipts it's real money. Which policy is correct depends on what actually happens in the world: if the bank converts each receipt separately (typical for card settlements), per-receipt is not a policy choice, it's a description - your books must match the bank's cents. If you hold euros and convert in bulk, bulk matches reality. Either way, the residual cent needs a home: a small 'FX rounding' account absorbs the difference between the converted book figures and the settled amounts, reviewed monthly. What you must never do is let the difference float unexplained or force it into a customer's balance. Rounding differences are a known cost of doing arithmetic in two currencies; named and housed, they're boring. Unnamed, they become reconciliation mysteries.
Why are you so insistent that the exchange rate gets stored on the entry itself? We have internet - anyone can look up what the euro was on March 10th.

They can look up A rate for March 10th. They cannot look up YOUR rate, and the difference is the whole argument. On any given day there are many defensible euro rates: the European Central Bank's daily reference, your bank's buying rate (which includes their spread), the card network's settlement rate, the rate at 9am versus the close. They differ by tenths of a percent - on EUR 500 that's a few dollars; on a year of European revenue it's thousands - and each produces a different dollar figure for the same payment. The bank statement will show exactly one of them: the amount that actually arrived. If the entry doesn't record which rate produced that amount, then next year an auditor, a partner, or future-you faces a dollar figure that no published rate quite reproduces, and a small mystery is born. Mysteries in ledgers compound; this one is preventable for the cost of one column.

There's a second, colder reason: rates get revised and sources vanish. Reference rates are occasionally restated, free rate APIs change their history or shut down, and 'the rate we used' from a spreadsheet someone deleted is gone for good. The entry is the one artifact guaranteed to survive as long as the books do. So the rule is total: amount in original currency, rate applied, source of the rate, resulting amount - recorded at the moment of conversion, on the entry, never reconstructed. A conversion you have to reconstruct is an opinion; a conversion recorded at the time is evidence.
Quick sanity check: our treasurer's summary says 'cash position: $3,450'. We hold EUR 2,300 and $1,150. Close enough for a summary, or is this actually wrong?

It's actually wrong, in an instructive way. EUR 2,300 plus $1,150 is $3,450 only if a euro is worth exactly one dollar - it isn't, and the summary has silently assumed parity. At, say, 1.08, the euro holding is worth $2,484, so the position expressed in dollars is about $3,634 - the summary understates it by $184. At 0.95 it would overstate. But the deeper problem isn't the arithmetic error; it's that a single blended number destroys information the business needs. Those two piles of money do different jobs: the euros pay the European supplier without conversion cost or timing risk; the dollars pay rent. 'Cash position $3,634 (converted)' can't tell you whether you can cover a EUR 2,500 invoice due Friday - the two-number version can, instantly (you're EUR 200 short and must convert or buy euros, whatever the dollar total says).

The honest format is two lines, always: EUR 2,300 and $1,150, each in its own currency, un-added. If a summary truly needs a single figure for a chart, it may show one - labeled as a conversion, with the rate and the date attached: '≈ $3,634 at 1.08, Mar 31'. The ≈ and the rate are not decoration; they're the difference between a fact and a derived estimate. A treasurer's summary that blends currencies without a rate is like a scale that reports your weight plus your height as one number: precise, confident, and meaningless.

But 'we made money on the exchange rate' implies a gain the business earned, and that framing misleads in two ways. First, there was no exchange-rate activity: you didn't hold euros speculating on a rise; you received revenue in euros and converted it when it arrived. Second, the mirror image is just as likely next month - had February's rate been 1.00, the same euros would have yielded $200, and nobody would say the business 'lost money on the exchange rate' as if a trade had gone wrong.

Full accounting systems DO name this difference - exchange gain or loss - and book it when foreign balances are revalued. At the level of these books, the honest treatment is the one you're looking at: record each conversion at its own rate on its own entry, let the difference be visible and explainable, and decline to book a gain or loss line for it. What you must not do is the third option some businesses drift into: converting both months at one 'standard' rate for tidiness. That would fabricate a dollar figure that matches neither bank deposit, and the $10 wouldn't vanish - it would go underground and reappear as a reconciliation break.

At 1.12, $880 converts to 78571.428... euro cents; applied to whole cents, 78571 - leaving a shortfall of 1429 euro cents, EUR 14.29, still owed. That residual is the instructive part. If you had to give me one rule for multi-currency bookkeeping that prevents 90% of the pain, what is it?

Store the original, treat every conversion as a dated opinion about it. The euro amount on a European invoice is a fact - it was printed on a document, agreed by two parties, and it will never change. The dollar figure next to it is a translation made at a particular rate on a particular day for a particular purpose (deposit matching, a report, a tax filing), and a different day or purpose can legitimately produce a different translation. Systems get into pain when they invert this: storing only the converted figure, or overwriting the original with a 'better' conversion later. Then the fact is gone and all that remains is an opinion nobody can audit, and when the bank's actual deposit disagrees with it - it will, by the spread alone - there's nothing left to reconcile against.

Everything else follows from the rule. Because the original is sacred, you never sum across currencies: sums only make sense within one fact-set. Because conversions are opinions, they carry their credentials: rate, source, date, purpose. Because opinions age, reports that show converted totals re-derive them at stated rates rather than reading a stale stored column. And when two conversions of the same item disagree - the bank's and the reference rate's - that's not an error to be resolved by deleting one; it's two opinions with different sources, and the books should say which one governs which purpose. Facts in the original currency, opinions labeled with their rates: keep that line bright and multi-currency stops being scary. Blur it, and no amount of careful arithmetic downstream will save you.

Three partners need to split a EUR 100 expense. If I split the euros and convert each share at 1.08, I get dollar figures that add to $108.01, but converting EUR 100 directly gives $108.00. Which numbers do I hand the partners?

Hand them the euro numbers, and let the dollar figure be a display, not a distribution. Split in the currency of the debt: EUR 100.00 is 10000 euro cents; three ways, the exact share is 3333.33..., so by largest remainder the shares are 3334, 3333, 3333 euro cents - EUR 33.34, 33.33, 33.33 - summing to exactly 10000. That split is final and provable. The dollars are where the phantom cent creeps in: converting each share at 1.08 gives 3334 x 1.08 = 3600.72, rounding to $36.01, and 3333 x 1.08 = 3599.64, rounding to $36.00, twice - total $108.01. Converting the whole 10000 x 1.08 = $108.00 exactly. Three roundings gained a cent that one rounding didn't, the same accumulation effect as any per-item conversion.

So the rule: split, allocate, and reconcile in the original currency, where exactness is achievable; convert once, at the end, for reporting, and convert totals rather than parts whenever a total is what's needed. If the partners are actually being reimbursed in dollars, then the thing being split is really a dollar obligation - convert the EUR 100 to $108.00 first, once, and split the dollars (3600 each, exactly) - the split currency should be the settlement currency. What you can't coherently do is split in one currency and settle in another while demanding both the split and the total be exact: the rounding cent has to belong to somebody, and the time to decide who is before anyone is owed anything.

A customer upgrades from our $30 plan to the $90 plan on February 11, 2026. What's the February charge? Don't use a 30-day month on me - February 2026 has 28 days, I checked.

You checked correctly - 2026 is not a leap year, so February 2026 has 28 days, and 28 is the denominator. The convention: the old plan covers the days before the change, the new plan covers the change day onward. Old plan, Feb 1-10, ten days: 3000 x 10/28 = 1071.43 cents, rounding to 1071. New plan, Feb 11-28, eighteen days: 9000 x 18/28 = 5785.71 cents, rounding to 5786. Total February charge: 1071 + 5786 = 6857 cents - $68.57. Sanity-check the shape: it's between a full month at the old price ($30) and a full month at the new ($90), much closer to the new price because 18 of the 28 days ran at $90 - a February upgrade lands fast, since the short month concentrates the expensive days.

Two conventions in there deserve to be explicit, because they're choices, not laws. The switch day belongs to the NEW plan (the customer got the new features on the 11th) - billing it to the old plan instead would move exactly one day, 9000/28 - 3000/28, about $2.14, and either choice is defensible if applied consistently. And each segment is rounded to cents independently, then added - rounding only the total would give 6857 here too (1071.43 + 5785.71 = 6857.14), but with other dates the two methods diverge by a cent, so the system should name one. Proration disputes are never about the formula; they're about a convention the customer never saw. Print the segments - days, dates, rates - on the invoice, and the math defends itself.
Same kind of switch in July instead: $50 plan to $80 plan, effective July 16. July has 31 days. What's the July charge?

Thirty-one in the denominator this time. The old plan covers July 1-15, fifteen days: 5000 x 15/31 = 2419.35 cents, rounding to 2419. The new plan covers July 16-31, sixteen days: 8000 x 16/31 = 4129.03 cents, rounding to 4129. Total: 2419 + 4129 = 6548 cents - $65.48. The shape check: the month is nearly half and half (15 days cheap, 16 days dear), and $65.48 sits nearly halfway between $50 and $80, leaning slightly toward $80 because the new plan got the extra day - exactly as it should.

Compare February's upgrade, where 18 of 28 days at the new price pulled the total to $68.57 on a $30-to-$90 jump: the longer month dilutes each day's weight (a July day is 1/31 of the month, a February day 1/28), so mid-month switches in long months land closer to the midpoint between the two prices. This is why 'just charge half and half for a mid-month switch' is wrong in both directions - it overcharges in February and undercharges across a 31-day month. The day-count method is one formula with no special cases: days at each price, over the true length of that month. Any system that hardcodes 30 has a small, systematic error that always favors whoever chose the constant - and customers eventually do the February math themselves.

Every billing system I touch prorates slightly differently and one of them definitely double-charges the switch day. What are the actual decisions hiding inside 'prorated by days', and which one causes the double-charge?

There are four decisions inside that innocent phrase, and yes, one of them is your double-charge. First, the denominator: the actual days in the month (28-31), a fixed 30, or a 365-day year divided into daily rates. Actual-days is the only one that's never systematically wrong. Second, the segments: which plan owns the switch day. The clean rule is old plan covers up to the day before the change, new plan covers the change day onward - the customer woke up with the new features, so the new plan bills that day. The double-charge bug is the overlap version: old plan billed THROUGH the switch day AND new plan billed FROM it, so day one of the new plan is charged twice - at both rates. Its mirror, the gap version, bills neither, and quietly gives a day away. With segments defined as [start, switch) and [switch, end], neither can happen: every day belongs to exactly one segment, by construction.

Third, rounding: per segment (then add) or once on the total - a cent of difference on some switches, so pick one and be consistent. Fourth, upgrades versus downgrades: many services prorate upgrades immediately but let downgrades take effect at the next cycle, which is a policy about revenue and resentment, not arithmetic - but it must be a stated policy, not an accident of implementation. The test for any proration engine is a one-line audit: for a switch on day k of an N-day month, the segments must cover k-1... precisely (switch day minus start) days at the old price and the remaining days at the new, summing to N days exactly. If a system's two segments ever sum to N+1 or N-1, you've found the bug - and it's always in the boundary day, never in the rates.

Same upgrade as your February example - $30 to $90 on February 11 - but in 2024 instead of 2026. A colleague says the charge is identical because 'it's the same dates'. Settle it.

Your colleague is wrong by 74 cents, and the reason is the calendar: 2024 was a leap year, so February 2024 had 29 days, not 28. Same dates, different month, different denominator. Run both. February 2026 (28 days): old plan Feb 1-10 is 3000 x 10/28 = 1071.43, rounding to 1071; new plan Feb 11-28, eighteen days, is 9000 x 18/28 = 5785.71, rounding to 5786; total $68.57. February 2024 (29 days): old plan is 3000 x 10/29 = 1034.48, rounding to 1034; new plan covers Feb 11-29, nineteen days - the leap day belongs to the new plan - at 9000 x 19/29 = 5896.55, rounding to 5897; total 1034 + 5897 = 6931 cents, $69.31. Difference: 6931 - 6857 = 74 cents, from nothing but the denominator and the extra day.

Both effects push the same way here: the extra day is a day at the expensive $90 rate (adding roughly $3.10 of new-plan time), while the longer month dilutes every day's price slightly (each old-plan day costs 3000/29 instead of 3000/28). This is the standing argument for computing proration from the real calendar - actual year, actual month length, actual switch date - rather than from a table of 'February = 28 days' constants. A hardcoded February breaks exactly once every four years, in the shortest month, on the customers most likely to be checking a leap-year invoice. Date arithmetic is one of the few things computers are genuinely better at than tables of constants; let the calendar be the calendar.

Our trial ends June 14 and billing anchors on the 1st of the month. Rather than start a weird mid-month cycle, we want to charge a stub for June 15-30 and then go monthly from July 1. The plan is $60. What's the stub?

The stub is just proration wearing a different hat - days used over days in the period, at the full plan price. June has 30 days; the paid stub covers June 15-30, which is 16 days (the 15th through the 30th inclusive - count them: 30 - 15 + 1 = 16). So the stub is 6000 x 16/30 = 3200 cents exactly - $32.00, no rounding drama this time. July 1 then starts the clean $60 monthly cycle on your anchor date, and the customer has paid for precisely the days they used and not one day more.

The alternatives show why the stub is the right shape. Charging the full $60 on June 15 for a cycle ending July 14 breaks your anchor permanently - this customer is now mid-month forever, and every future proration, report, and cohort analysis inherits the skew. Waiving the stub and starting July 1 gives away 16 days - over half a month - and scales terribly: at a thousand trial conversions a month, that's real revenue surrendered to a calendar preference. And back-billing June 15-30 inside the July invoice as an unexplained $92 line is how you generate 'why is my first bill wrong?' tickets. The stub keeps three things true at once: the anchor date survives, the customer pays for exactly their usage, and the invoice can show its work - 'Jun 15-30, 16 of 30 days at $60: $32.00' - in one line. Trials end on random dates; anchors shouldn't have to.

Our suspense account has $23 sitting in it from the March reconciliation that we never identified. My partner wants to zero it to 'miscellaneous income' so the close looks clean. Talk me out of it - or tell me he's right.

He's wrong, and the $23 is exactly why the suspense account exists. Suspense is a labeled parking place for amounts that are real - the bank moved money, the books must reflect it - but unexplained. Parking the 2300 there during the close was correct. Sweeping it into income to make the account zero is something else: it fabricates $23 of revenue that no customer paid, it destroys the trail (next quarter, nobody can find the discrepancy because it's been dissolved into a thousand legitimate income lines), and it teaches the worst possible lesson - that unexplained differences get absorbed rather than explained, at $23 this quarter and at $2,300 the quarter someone stops paying attention. The amount is trivial. The precedent is the entire control system.

The honest treatment has three parts. Carry the balance, disclosed: the close package lists 'suspense: $23.00, one unidentified bank item from March, under investigation'. Keep investigating proportionately - $23 earns an hour, not an audit; most such items turn out to be a bank fee variant or a mis-keyed deposit, and they tend to identify themselves when a customer or statement surfaces. And if it ages past your policy threshold - many firms use 90 days - it gets written off then, by a named decision, to a named account, with the story attached, not silently during a busy close. A suspense account at zero because everything got explained is a sign of health. A suspense account at zero because everything got swept is a rug, and everyone who's worked a close knows what's under rugs. The close doesn't require zero; it requires explained - and 'unexplained, $23, carried and disclosed' IS an explanation of the state of knowledge.

Our bookkeeper says March is 'closed'. What does that actually commit us to? People keep asking her to 'just slip one more invoice into March'.

Closed is a promise about the past: the March numbers that were reported - to you, to partners, to the bank, to the tax file - will not change underneath the people who used them. Concretely it means three things. The period is locked against new entries dated in March: the late invoice gets an April date (or is accrued properly if it truly belongs to March's economics and the close hasn't finalized - that's what the pre-close checklist is for). Corrections to March, when they're genuinely needed, are made as entries in the open period that reference March, so both the original reports and the correction remain visible - the record shows 'March as reported' and 'March as corrected' instead of a March that silently mutated. And the closing balances become the opening balances of April, so a changed March would ripple forward through every subsequent month - the lock is what makes the chain trustworthy.

The 'just slip it in' requests are the reason the concept exists. Each one is individually tiny and reasonable, and collectively they mean no report is ever final, no two printouts of 'March' ever agree, and nobody can say which version a decision was based on. The professional answer to give the requesters: the invoice absolutely gets recorded - today, in April, with its true date noted - and if it's material to March's story, it's disclosed alongside the March reports. Closed doesn't mean March was perfect. It means March is stable, and stability is what makes the numbers safe to build on.

We bought equipment for $6,000 cash in January 2025. It doesn't appear in any month's expenses, which makes every month look cheaper than it is. Someone mentioned depreciation. Give me the mechanics, not the tax lecture.

Mechanics only. The $6,000 bought an asset - equipment - not a January expense, because the machine serves for years. Depreciation is the discipline of moving its cost into expense gradually, in step with its use. The simplest method, straight-line over an estimated life: say five years, no salvage value. Monthly charge: 600000 cents / 60 months = 10000 cents - $100.00 - booked every month as an entry: debit Depreciation Expense 10000, credit Accumulated Depreciation 10000. Accumulated depreciation is a contra-asset: it sits against the equipment account, reducing its book value without touching the original cost record. After fourteen months, accumulated depreciation is 14 x 10000 = 140000, and the machine's book value is 600000 - 140000 = 460000 - $4,600.00 - which is the books' current claim about what the machine is worth to the business.

Three things this achieves. Every month now carries $100 of the machine's cost, so monthly profit stops flattering itself. The balance sheet tells a decaying, honest story about the asset instead of pretending a five-year-old machine is worth its purchase price until the day it's scrapped. And when the machine is sold or retired, the gain or loss falls out of the numbers already there - sale price versus book value - rather than arriving as a surprise. The estimates inside it (five years, no salvage) are judgments, stated once and applied consistently; different methods - declining balance front-loads the expense - change the timing, never the total: over the machine's life, exactly $6,000 of expense will be recognized, no more, no less. Depreciation is allocation, not valuation magic - and allocation is what keeps each month honest.
Give me a month-end close sequence I can actually run a small business on - in the order the steps have to happen, with why the order matters.

Four steps, in an order that is not negotiable, because each step's output is the next step's input. One: cutoff. Stop the inflow - all March invoices entered, all March receipts recorded, bank feeds imported through March 31. Nothing downstream means anything if the population of transactions is still changing, so the close starts by freezing the guest list. Two: accruals and adjustments. Book the entries that belong to March but haven't touched cash - wages earned but unpaid, the month's slice of prepaid insurance, depreciation, revenue earned but not yet invoiced. These come before reconciliation because they change the book balances the reconciliation will test. Three: reconciliation. Bank against books, clearing accounts against processor reports, suspense examined line by line. This is the verification step, and it only works on complete, adjusted books - reconcile first and your accruals land afterwards as brand-new unexplained differences. Four: review and lock. Read the statements as a story - does March's profit make sense against March's activity? - run the integrity checks (journals balanced, no orphans, suspense explained or disclosed), then lock the period.

The failure mode this ordering prevents is the circular close: adjusting after reconciling, reconciling after reporting, 'final' numbers that change three times. Each violation costs more than the step it skipped, because the steps downstream have to be redone on the new numbers. A small business can run this in an afternoon - the sequence matters far more than the scale. Cutoff, accruals, reconciliation, review, lock. Print it, tape it to the wall, and let the calendar be boring.
